R.name: Realistic
R.tagline: Practical action, tools, materials, equipment and visible results
R.definition: Realistic interest reflects attraction to hands-on activity: making, repairing, operating, growing, moving or working directly with physical systems. The theme concerns what a learner may enjoy doing; it does not prove mechanical skill, physical strength or a preference for low-complexity work.
lens: Building or assembling; troubleshooting equipment; working outdoors; using tools or machines; handling materials; operating technical systems; producing a concrete result.
Clear tasks, tangible feedback, practical problem solving, physical or field activity and opportunities to learn by doing.
Long periods of purely abstract discussion, ambiguous outputs or work detached from observable application may feel less energising. This is a possibility to test, not a rule.
R.careers: Engineering workshops, skilled trades, agriculture, logistics, manufacturing, field technology, aviation, construction, environmental operations, emergency services and laboratory support. These examples refer to activity patterns, not a guaranteed fit. Each field contains multiple roles and requires its own qualifications, abilities, values and opportunities.
actions: Complete a supervised build, repair or field project.
Interview a technician or engineer about a normal workday.
Compare enjoyment of design, operation, maintenance and outdoor work rather than treating them as one activity.
R.reflection: Which recent activity shows genuine realistic interest, and what part of that activity was actually enjoyable?

I.name: Investigative
I.tagline: Inquiry, evidence, analysis, explanation and discovery
I.definition: Investigative interest reflects attraction to questions that require observation, research, diagnosis, modelling or evidence-based explanation. It is not an intelligence score and does not mean that the learner must pursue science or enjoy every kind of academic study.
lens: Researching causes; analysing data; testing ideas; diagnosing problems; reading technical material; designing investigations; explaining complex systems.
Time to think, access to information, meaningful questions, intellectual challenge and permission to revise a conclusion when evidence changes.
Repetitive activity with no problem to solve, unsupported claims or constant action without analysis may feel less engaging.
I.careers: Science, medicine and health research, data analytics, computing, economics, psychology research, policy analysis, environmental science, laboratories and technical consulting. These examples refer to activity patterns, not a guaranteed fit. Each field contains multiple roles and requires its own qualifications, abilities, values and opportunities.
actions: Investigate one question using at least two evidence sources.
Try a data, laboratory, coding or research-method task.
Ask a professional how uncertainty is handled in their field.
I.reflection: Which recent activity shows genuine investigative interest, and what part of that activity was actually enjoyable?

A.name: Artistic
A.tagline: Original expression, imagination, design and open-ended creation
A.definition: Artistic interest reflects attraction to creating, interpreting or communicating original ideas and experiences. It may appear through visual design, writing, performance, media, storytelling, food, fashion or concept development. It is broader than fine arts and is not a judgement of talent.
lens: Writing or storytelling; visual or interaction design; performance; composing; creative direction; producing media; inventing forms, experiences or messages.
Choice in how to approach a task, space for experimentation, meaningful expression, exposure to ideas and constructive feedback on original work.
Highly prescribed tasks with one permitted method, repetitive routines or environments that discourage experimentation may feel less attractive.
A.careers: Design, media, writing, advertising, animation, architecture, user experience, content strategy, performing arts, fashion, publishing, creative technology and cultural work. These examples refer to activity patterns, not a guaranteed fit. Each field contains multiple roles and requires its own qualifications, abilities, values and opportunities.
actions: Produce a small portfolio piece for a real audience.
Compare solo creation with collaborative production.
Request feedback on both originality and usefulness.
A.reflection: Which recent activity shows genuine artistic interest, and what part of that activity was actually enjoyable?

S.name: Social
S.tagline: Helping, teaching, guiding, caring and developing people
S.definition: Social interest reflects attraction to activities that support learning, health, development, inclusion or wellbeing. It does not mean a learner is automatically highly sociable, emotionally skilled or suited to every service role; the nature and intensity of contact matter.
lens: Teaching; coaching; listening; counselling support; caring; facilitating; explaining; resolving needs; strengthening community or team capability.
Meaningful human impact, respectful relationships, opportunities to explain or support and feedback that another person or group has benefited.
Isolated work with little human purpose, competitive interaction without service value or constant exposure to intense needs without support may feel draining.
S.careers: Education, healthcare, counselling, social work, learning and development, human resources, community programs, customer success, public health and rehabilitation. These examples refer to activity patterns, not a guaranteed fit. Each field contains multiple roles and requires its own qualifications, abilities, values and opportunities.
actions: Tutor, mentor or facilitate a short learning activity.
Observe the difference between helping, teaching, caring and persuading.
Ask a practitioner about emotional load, boundaries and supervision.
S.reflection: Which recent activity shows genuine social interest, and what part of that activity was actually enjoyable?

E.name: Enterprising
E.tagline: Influence, initiative, negotiation, enterprise and leadership
E.definition: Enterprising interest reflects attraction to mobilising people and resources toward an outcome through persuasion, decision making, selling, leading or creating ventures. It does not establish ethical judgement, leadership ability, business knowledge or a desire for formal authority.
lens: Pitching ideas; negotiating; organising people; selling; campaigning; setting direction; launching initiatives; making commercial or strategic decisions.
Visible goals, autonomy, responsibility, contact with stakeholders, scope to influence outcomes and feedback through results.
Roles with no decision scope, little contact, limited ownership or procedures that block all initiative may feel less engaging.
E.careers: Business development, entrepreneurship, management, sales, marketing, politics and public affairs, fundraising, law, consulting, partnerships and project leadership. These examples refer to activity patterns, not a guaranteed fit. Each field contains multiple roles and requires its own qualifications, abilities, values and opportunities.
actions: Pitch a useful idea and record the questions it receives.
Lead a small project with clear success criteria.
Compare enjoyment of selling, negotiating, organising and taking financial risk.
E.reflection: Which recent activity shows genuine enterprising interest, and what part of that activity was actually enjoyable?

C.name: Conventional
C.tagline: Structure, accuracy, records, procedures and orderly information
C.definition: Conventional interest reflects attraction to organising information, applying dependable procedures and maintaining accuracy or control. It does not mean a learner lacks creativity, prefers low-status work or should be placed only in administration.
lens: Organising records; checking details; budgeting; scheduling; processing transactions; applying regulations; managing data; maintaining reliable workflows.
Clear standards, dependable systems, accurate information, visible completion, defined responsibilities and opportunities to improve orderly processes.
Constantly changing expectations, missing information, avoidable disorder or roles where accuracy is undervalued may reduce engagement.
C.careers: Finance, accounting, banking operations, administration, compliance, data management, supply-chain planning, quality systems, legal operations, records and project control. These examples refer to activity patterns, not a guaranteed fit. Each field contains multiple roles and requires its own qualifications, abilities, values and opportunities.
actions: Design a simple tracking or budgeting system.
Shadow a role where accuracy prevents real harm or loss.
Compare enjoyment of data, finance, scheduling, regulation and process improvement.
C.reflection: Which recent activity shows genuine conventional interest, and what part of that activity was actually enjoyable?

bands.label: Emerging practice
bands.meaning: Behaviour was endorsed less often in this administration

bands.label: Developing practice
bands.meaning: Behaviour may appear in selected situations

bands.label: Strong practice signal
bands.meaning: Behaviour was frequently endorsed

bands.label: Distinctive practice signal
bands.meaning: Behaviour was very frequently endorsed

SAW.name: Self-Awareness
SAW.tagline: Recognising emotions, triggers and their effect on judgement
SAW.definition: Self-Awareness describes how clearly a learner reports noticing and naming current emotions, recognising common triggers and observing how mood may influence decisions or behaviour. It is not introspection alone, self-confidence, honesty, or a mental-health screen.
lens: Names emotions with useful precision; notices bodily and situational cues; identifies triggers; links mood with attention and judgement; checks personal impact before acting.
Time to pause, psychologically safe reflection, specific feedback, emotion vocabulary and recent examples rather than abstract self-description.
Creates an earlier decision point: the learner can notice an emotional signal before it automatically shapes communication or action.

May become rumination, excessive self-monitoring or repeated analysis without action. When less visible: May notice an emotion only after the reaction, confuse intensity with accuracy or overlook the effect of mood on choices.
SAW.careers: Learning, counselling, creative work, leadership development, client service and any setting where reflection and feedback improve decisions. These examples require separate evidence of interest, aptitude, qualifications, values and opportunity.
actions: Use a three-part check once a day: emotion, trigger and likely action urge.
Before an important decision, record what evidence is independent of the current mood.
Ask a trusted person for one example of how your emotional state affected a recent interaction.
SAW.reflection: Which emotion was easiest to recognise this week, and which signal did you miss until later?

SRG.name: Self-Regulation
SRG.tagline: Pausing, managing impulses and choosing a constructive response
SRG.definition: Self-Regulation describes how often a learner reports creating space between emotion and action, managing impulses and choosing behaviour that protects the goal and the people involved. It does not mean suppressing emotion, staying calm at all times or tolerating mistreatment.
lens: Pauses when provoked; reduces impulsive reactions; reframes a situation; uses coping routines; communicates frustration without directing it at others; recovers and re-engages.
Clear boundaries, access to healthy regulation strategies, permission to pause, realistic workload and support when demands exceed ordinary coping.
Protects decision quality and relationships when emotion is intense, without treating emotion as an enemy.

May become emotional masking, avoidance of necessary expression or appearing controlled while stress accumulates. When less visible: May react before checking consequences, direct frustration at others or abandon a useful plan during a temporary emotional peak.
SRG.careers: Customer service, healthcare, operations, education, negotiation, project delivery and roles involving feedback, uncertainty or pressure. These examples require separate evidence of interest, aptitude, qualifications, values and opportunity.
actions: Practise one ninety-second pause routine before responding to a low-risk frustration.
Write a respectful boundary sentence for a situation that usually triggers an impulsive response.
After a difficult event, compare the action urge with the action that best serves the longer-term goal.
SRG.reflection: What helps you pause without denying what you feel?

IMO.name: Internal Motivation
IMO.tagline: Purposeful effort, persistence and self-directed momentum
IMO.definition: Internal Motivation describes how often a learner reports connecting effort to a meaningful goal, restarting after setbacks and creating momentum without constant external prompting. It is a competency in Career Garage's mixed framework, not a pure emotional ability and not proof of ambition, discipline or future success.
lens: Connects tasks to purpose; starts without repeated prompting; persists through uneven progress; learns from setbacks; protects attention; revises the route without abandoning the goal automatically.
Meaningful goals, visible progress, appropriate challenge, autonomy, feedback and practical support for barriers outside the learner's control.
Helps translate emotional information and personal meaning into sustained, goal-directed action.

May become overwork, self-pressure, refusal to rest or persistence with a goal that evidence no longer supports. When less visible: May depend heavily on reminders, stop after slow progress or struggle to connect daily tasks with a valued outcome.
IMO.careers: Long-cycle study, research, entrepreneurship, project work, skill development, independent assignments and roles requiring sustained follow-through. These examples require separate evidence of interest, aptitude, qualifications, values and opportunity.
actions: Link one weekly task to the learner outcome or value it serves.
Turn a delayed goal into a fifteen-minute restart action with a visible completion point.
Set a review rule that distinguishes useful persistence from continuing only because time was already invested.
IMO.reflection: Which goal creates energy because it matters to you, and what is the smallest evidence-building step?

EMP.name: Empathy
EMP.tagline: Noticing emotional cues and considering another perspective
EMP.definition: Empathy describes how often a learner reports noticing possible emotional cues, considering another person's perspective and adjusting a response with respect. It does not prove that an inference is correct, require agreement, remove boundaries or authorise reading hidden motives.
lens: Listens for meaning and emotion; notices mismatches between words and cues; considers context; checks an interpretation; adapts tone; distinguishes understanding from agreement.
Curiosity, time to listen, cultural humility, permission to ask rather than assume and boundaries that prevent emotional over-involvement.
Improves the quality of questions, service and collaboration by keeping another person's experience in view.

May become emotional over-identification, weak boundaries, assumption disguised as understanding or avoidance of necessary challenge. When less visible: May miss discomfort, minimise a different emotional response or make people-centred decisions without enough input from the people affected.
EMP.careers: Education, healthcare, counselling support, design research, customer experience, community work, human resources and collaborative leadership. These examples require separate evidence of interest, aptitude, qualifications, values and opportunity.
actions: Replace one assumption with a checking question: 'Am I understanding this correctly?'
Summarise the other person's perspective before explaining your own.
Practise an empathy boundary: understand the concern, name your role and agree on the next responsible action.
EMP.reflection: When did asking instead of assuming change your understanding of someone?

RMG.name: Relationship Management
RMG.tagline: Clear communication, feedback, influence and conflict repair
RMG.definition: Relationship Management describes how often a learner reports addressing tension, communicating respectfully, giving useful feedback and helping people move toward constructive action. It does not measure popularity, compliance, charisma or the absence of conflict.
lens: Raises issues early; gives specific feedback; listens and responds; clarifies shared outcomes; repairs misunderstandings; negotiates next steps; follows through on relational commitments.
Clear norms, mutual respect, psychological safety, fair power boundaries, permission to disagree and accountability for harmful behaviour.
Turns awareness and regulation into observable interaction that can preserve trust while still addressing a real issue.

May become over-managing others, harmony seeking, persuasive pressure or taking responsibility for relationships that require reciprocal effort. When less visible: May avoid necessary conversations, allow tension to grow or communicate a valid concern in a way that blocks joint action.
RMG.careers: Team leadership, teaching, partnerships, client work, project coordination, sales, service recovery, negotiation and community programs. These examples require separate evidence of interest, aptitude, qualifications, values and opportunity.
actions: Use an observation-impact-request structure in one low-risk feedback conversation.
Address a small tension within forty-eight hours instead of waiting for certainty or frustration.
End a difficult conversation with the agreed action, owner, timing and follow-up point.
RMG.reflection: Which relationship would benefit from one clear, respectful conversation this week?

bands.label: Lower current priority
bands.meaning: This condition was less important within the response pattern

bands.label: Considered priority
bands.meaning: The condition matters but may be negotiable

bands.label: Strong priority
bands.meaning: The condition should be investigated in opportunity comparisons

bands.label: Defining priority
bands.meaning: The condition may strongly shape current decisions and trade-offs

ACH.name: Achievement
ACH.tagline: Challenge, mastery, visible progress and meaningful accomplishment
ACH.definition: Achievement describes how important it is for a learner to use abilities fully, master demanding responsibilities and see evidence that effort produced a worthwhile result. It is a work-reward priority, not a measure of talent, grades, competitiveness or future success.
lens: Seeks stretching goals; notices progress; wants standards for a strong result; values mastery; prefers work where contribution and completion are visible.
Real challenge, achievable standards, useful feedback, enough resources, visible milestones and recognition of contribution without turning every task into a contest.
Directs attention toward roles that provide mastery, progress and a clear sense of accomplishment.
Can conflict with Security when growth requires uncertainty, or with Relationships when competitive systems reward individual results over shared success.
A lower current priority may mean the learner values other conditions more; it does not mean low ambition or weak performance.
ACH.careers: Project-based work, research, performance improvement, professional practice, entrepreneurship, technical mastery and roles with clear outcomes.
actions: Compare two roles by the challenge, feedback and completion evidence each provides.
Ask a professional how progress is defined during the first year in the role.
Run a short project that produces a visible result and record which parts felt rewarding.
ACH.reflection: What kind of accomplishment would make a difficult year of learning feel worthwhile?

AUT.name: Autonomy
AUT.tagline: Choice, ownership, judgement and latitude in how work is completed
AUT.definition: Autonomy describes how important it is for a learner to have meaningful choice, responsibility and room to use judgement when planning and completing work. It does not mean working alone, rejecting supervision, ignoring standards or having no accountability.
lens: Values decision latitude; prefers ownership of an approach; wants reasons rather than only instructions; likes flexibility within clear outcomes; accepts responsibility for choices.
Clear goals, appropriate authority, access to information, trust, feedback, transparent boundaries and competence matched to the level of independence.
Helps distinguish roles that permit self-direction from those built around tightly prescribed procedures.
Can conflict with Security when independent paths are less predictable, or with Relationships when autonomy is mistaken for isolation.
A lower current priority may reflect comfort with structure, collaboration or guided learning; it does not imply dependence or weak initiative.
AUT.careers: Consulting, design, research, entrepreneurship, skilled professional practice, field roles and accountable positions with outcome-based supervision.
actions: Ask how decisions, approvals and ownership are divided in a target role.
Complete one project with a self-designed plan and request feedback on the outcome.
Separate the freedom you want from the standards and accountability you are willing to accept.
AUT.reflection: Which decisions do you want to own, and which guidance would help you use that freedom well?

SEC.name: Security
SEC.tagline: Predictability, continuity, dependable income and clear working conditions
SEC.definition: Security describes how important dependable employment, predictable income, clear expectations and continuity are when evaluating work. It is not fearfulness, low risk tolerance in every domain or a guarantee that a particular employer will remain stable.
lens: Checks contract and continuity; values dependable pay and benefits; prefers clear expectations; considers organisational resilience; notices risk and transition support.
Transparent terms, lawful employment, financial predictability, safe work, fair policies, credible continuity and honest communication about change.
Makes practical constraints visible so career planning does not confuse aspiration with avoidable financial or employment risk.
Can conflict with Growth and Variety or Autonomy when new opportunities involve temporary uncertainty; the trade-off depends on obligations and risk capacity.
A lower current priority may reflect flexibility or greater risk capacity; it does not prove recklessness and should never be used to justify unsafe work.
SEC.careers: Established organisations, regulated sectors, public service, essential services, long-term programmes and roles with clear contracts and progression structures.
actions: Define the minimum income, benefit, location and continuity conditions your plan must meet.
Compare advertised stability with evidence such as contract type, turnover and funding model.
Build one risk-managed experiment before rejecting a growth opportunity as too uncertain.
SEC.reflection: Which forms of stability are essential now, and which uncertainty could you manage with preparation?

IMP.name: Service and Impact
IMP.tagline: Purpose, positive contribution and a beneficiary the learner can respect
IMP.definition: Service and Impact describes how important it is for work to address a real human, community or environmental need and contribute to a purpose the learner can respect. It does not require unpaid work, self-sacrifice, one particular sector or agreement with every organisational claim.
lens: Asks who benefits; examines mission and consequences; values useful contribution; wants ethical coherence; looks for evidence that work solves a real problem.
Credible purpose, responsible practice, visible beneficiaries, ethical safeguards, sustainable workload and evidence that impact claims match operations.
Adds meaning and social consequence to career comparison instead of evaluating roles only by title, salary or prestige.
Can conflict with Security or Achievement when mission-led roles offer fewer resources or slower visible results; purpose should not erase fair-pay and safety needs.
A lower current priority does not mean selfishness or weak ethics; contribution may be expressed outside paid work or through responsible performance in any sector.
IMP.careers: Healthcare, education, public service, sustainability, social enterprise, responsible technology, community development and mission-led functions in any sector.
actions: Write a one-sentence impact hypothesis for a target role: action, beneficiary and evidence.
Interview someone doing the work and ask where the mission is visible in ordinary tasks.
Check whether the organisation's policies, incentives and outcomes support its public purpose.
IMP.reflection: Whose problem do you want your work to help solve, and what evidence would show real benefit?

REL.name: Relationships
REL.tagline: Respect, trust, belonging, cooperation and supportive contact
REL.definition: Relationships describes how important respectful, trustworthy and supportive working relationships are to a learner. It does not mean needing constant social contact, avoiding disagreement, being popular or accepting poor boundaries in the name of teamwork.
lens: Values trust and belonging; prefers respectful communication; notices cooperation and credit-sharing; wants reliable support; considers team climate when judging a role.
Fair treatment, psychological safety, inclusive norms, constructive conflict, reciprocal support, clear boundaries and leaders who address harmful behaviour.
Keeps social climate visible because the same occupation can feel very different across teams, supervisors and organisations.
Can conflict with Achievement in highly competitive settings or with Autonomy when collaboration becomes constant coordination; healthy fit preserves both connection and boundaries.
A lower current priority may reflect preference for task focus or independent work; it does not mean poor social skill or lack of care for others.
REL.careers: Collaborative teams, education, health and care, community programmes, client partnerships, people operations and organisations with strong support cultures.
actions: Ask how teams share credit, handle disagreement and support new members.
Observe one target workplace or project team and record behavioural evidence of trust.
Define the relationship conditions you require separately from a wish for universal harmony.
REL.reflection: What observable team behaviour would make you feel respected and able to contribute?

GRV.name: Growth and Variety
GRV.tagline: Learning, development, novelty and changing challenges
GRV.definition: Growth and Variety describes how important ongoing learning, exposure to different challenges and a visible path for development are to a learner. It does not mean disliking routine, changing jobs frequently or needing constant excitement.
lens: Looks for learning access; values skill development; prefers some changing challenge; asks about rotation and progression; notices whether work expands future options.
Stretch with support, learning resources, feedback, varied exposure, mobility pathways and enough continuity to convert experience into competence.
Highlights whether a role can keep building capability and future options rather than only satisfying immediate conditions.
Can conflict with Security when development requires movement or with Relationships when rotation changes teams; variety without depth can also weaken mastery.
A lower current priority may reflect satisfaction with depth, continuity or familiar craft; it does not imply resistance to all learning.
GRV.careers: Consulting, technology, research, graduate programmes, rotational roles, creative production, entrepreneurship and rapidly evolving professional fields.
actions: Compare roles by first-year learning, feedback, rotation and progression opportunities.
Test a new task for four weeks while tracking energy, learning and desire for deeper practice.
Ask whether advertised variety builds transferable capability or only adds fragmented workload.
GRV.reflection: Which kind of variety builds the future capability you most want, rather than only preventing boredom?

bands.label: Lower current preference
bands.meaning: This method was less strongly endorsed in the response pattern

bands.label: Context-dependent preference
bands.meaning: The method may help in some tasks or conditions

bands.label: Regular preference
bands.meaning: The method often feels useful and is worth testing deliberately

bands.label: Strongly expressed preference
bands.meaning: The method feels especially useful now but should not become an exclusive style

VIS.name: Visual Organisation
VIS.tagline: Seeing relationships, structure, position and sequence clearly
VIS.definition: Visual Organisation describes a current preference for arranging information through diagrams, maps, timelines, tables, colour, spatial position and other visible structures. It does not mean the learner has a fixed visual type, superior visual memory or a need for pictures in every task.
lens: Visible structure, relationships, grouping, sequence and overview
Concept maps, annotated diagrams, process charts, worked layouts, timelines and well-designed slides
Decorating notes without thinking, copying diagrams passively or assuming every idea is best represented visually
A lower score may mean words, practice or stepwise reflection feel more useful; it is not a visual-ability deficit
actions: Convert one chapter into a one-page concept map, then retrieve it from memory.
Compare a decorative diagram with a labelled explanatory diagram and test recall.
Use a timeline or flowchart only when sequence or relationship is central to the task.
VIS.reflection: Which relationship becomes clearer when you draw it, and how will you test whether the drawing improved learning?

VER.name: Verbal Explanation
VER.tagline: Building meaning through reading, writing, discussion and explanation
VER.definition: Verbal Explanation describes a current preference for processing ideas through words: reading, writing, questioning, discussion, self-explanation and teaching another person. It does not mean listening alone is sufficient or that the learner should avoid diagrams and practice.
lens: Clear language, definitions, reasoning, questions, dialogue and explanatory links
Self-explanation, summaries from memory, teach-back, question generation, discussion and structured notes
Rereading fluently without retrieval, producing long notes with little selection or mistaking talk for mastery
A lower score may mean words alone feel insufficient; it is not a language, reading or intelligence deficit
actions: Explain a difficult idea without notes, identify gaps and revise the explanation.
Write three why/how questions and answer them in plain language.
Use a study partner for teach-back, then complete an independent retrieval check.
VER.reflection: Can you explain the idea accurately without looking, and which part of your explanation still needs evidence?

ACT.name: Active Experience
ACT.tagline: Learning through purposeful application, rehearsal, demonstration and feedback
ACT.definition: Active Experience describes a current preference for trying, applying, rehearsing, experimenting or demonstrating a skill in a realistic task. Activity is useful when it requires relevant thinking and feedback; being busy, clicking, moving or watching a demonstration is not automatically learning.
lens: Practice, examples, manipulation, simulation, experimentation and visible consequences
Worked problems, labs, role plays, projects, prototypes, demonstrations, simulations and deliberate rehearsal
Trial without explanation, practice without feedback, repeating errors or avoiding foundational knowledge
A lower score may mean preparation and observation are preferred before action; it is not low motivation or practical ability
actions: Turn one concept into a small task with a clear success criterion.
Practise a difficult step, obtain feedback and repeat only after correcting the error.
Predict an outcome before an experiment, then explain the difference between prediction and result.
ACT.reflection: What can you safely try now, and what evidence will show that the practice improved performance?

REF.name: Reflective Structure
REF.tagline: Planning, sequencing, monitoring understanding and learning from review
REF.definition: Reflective Structure describes a current preference for pausing, organising a sequence, monitoring understanding, reviewing errors and planning the next learning step. Reflection is productive when it changes a strategy or decision; delay, overplanning and repeated review without action are not the goal.
lens: Time to think, ordered steps, criteria, progress monitoring and error review
Study plans, worked sequences, error logs, self-checks, learning journals, rubrics and post-task reflection
Overplanning, perfectionism, avoiding timely practice or reflecting without testing a revised approach
A lower score may mean the learner prefers quicker interaction or practice; it is not carelessness or weak metacognition
actions: Use a before-during-after plan for one study session.
Keep an error log that records cause, correction and the next retrieval date.
Set a short reflection limit, then convert the insight into one changed action.
REF.reflection: What did the last attempt reveal, and which specific change will you test next?

bands.label: Emerging confidence
bands.meaning: Provide access, modelling and a supported foundation task

bands.label: Developing confidence
bands.meaning: Practise core behaviours and verify with a simple rubric

bands.label: Strong confidence
bands.meaning: Test independent performance and transfer

bands.label: Highly expressed confidence
bands.meaning: Seek counter-evidence and verify responsible execution

IDL.name: Information and Data Literacy
IDL.tagline: Finding, evaluating, organising and interpreting digital information and data
IDL.definition: Information and Data Literacy is confidence in defining an information need, searching effectively, evaluating sources and evidence, organising files or data, and recognising incomplete or misleading claims. It does not certify research expertise or guarantee that a judgement is correct.
lens: Relevant evidence, source quality, context, data meaning, retrievability and traceability
Search plans, lateral reading, source comparison, file naming, data dictionaries and simple analysis
Information overload, endless searching, confirmation bias or confusing a polished source with a reliable one
A lower score may reflect limited access, language, instruction or practice; it is not low intelligence
actions: Use three different search formulations and record which produces the strongest evidence.
Compare author, date, purpose, evidence and corroboration for three sources on one claim.
Create a folder and file-naming system, then retrieve five items without browsing manually.
IDL.reflection: What evidence makes this source or dataset fit for the decision you are making?

DCC.name: Digital Communication and Collaboration
DCC.tagline: Communicating clearly, choosing suitable channels and collaborating responsibly online
DCC.definition: Digital Communication and Collaboration is confidence in selecting an appropriate channel, writing for the intended audience, contributing in shared workspaces, managing permissions and working respectfully across distance. It is not a measure of popularity, sociability or spoken-language ability.
lens: Audience, purpose, channel fit, clarity, shared ownership, feedback, boundaries and security
Email and chat conventions, shared documents, version notes, meeting records and access controls
Over-communication, unclear tone, accidental disclosure, exclusion, harassment or untracked decisions
A lower score may reflect limited opportunity or platform familiarity rather than poor teamwork
actions: Rewrite one message for chat, email and a formal shared document; explain the channel choice.
Use comments, task owners and a decision log in a small group project.
Audit the audience and permissions before sharing a file or link.
DCC.reflection: Can the intended audience understand, act and collaborate without receiving unnecessary information?

DCR.name: Digital Content Creation
DCR.tagline: Creating clear, accessible and lawful digital material for a defined purpose
DCR.definition: Digital Content Creation is confidence in planning, producing, formatting and revising documents, presentations, visuals or media for a specific audience. It includes attribution, permissions and accessibility. It does not measure artistic talent or professional production mastery.
lens: Purpose, audience, structure, clarity, accuracy, accessibility, ownership and revision evidence
Documents, slides, spreadsheets, visuals, audio/video, templates, captions and source records
Decoration without meaning, copying without permission, misinformation, inaccessible design or hidden AI use
A lower score may reflect tool access or exposure; it is not proof of low creativity
actions: Create a one-page explanation for a defined audience and test whether two users understand it.
Add headings, alt text, captions, readable contrast and a source list to an existing artifact.
Document the title, author, source, licence and changes for reused material.
DCR.reflection: Does this artifact communicate accurately, accessibly and lawfully to its intended audience?

DSP.name: Safety and Privacy
DSP.tagline: Protecting accounts, devices, personal information and other people in digital environments
DSP.definition: Safety and Privacy is confidence in using strong authentication, checking sharing settings, recognising suspicious requests, protecting sensitive data and responding to incidents. A high score does not guarantee security or qualify a learner as a cybersecurity professional.
lens: Least disclosure, verification, strong authentication, updates, backups, secure sharing and recovery
Password managers, multi-factor authentication, phishing checks, privacy settings and incident routes
False confidence, unsafe testing, victim blaming, oversharing screenshots or trying to investigate alone
A lower score is a priority for supported practice, not evidence of blame or irresponsibility
actions: Review account recovery, multi-factor authentication and unique-password coverage with an approved adult.
Classify practice messages as trusted, suspicious or unsafe and explain the verification step.
Write a lost-device or compromised-account response card using official support routes.
DSP.reflection: What must be verified before you click, share, install, pay or disclose information?

DPS.name: Digital Problem Solving
DPS.tagline: Learning tools, diagnosing common problems and choosing safe troubleshooting steps
DPS.definition: Digital Problem Solving is confidence in breaking a technical problem into smaller checks, interpreting error information, testing reversible steps, learning a new tool and knowing when to seek help. It is not a coding aptitude or professional technical-support certificate.
lens: Symptoms, context, recent change, probable causes, reversible tests, documentation and escalation
Checklists, safe restarts, settings review, error searches, help documentation and learning by testing
Random changes, data loss, unauthorised access, unsafe downloads or continuing beyond competence
A lower score may reflect anxiety or limited practice; it is not evidence of low reasoning ability
actions: Use a symptom-context-change-test-result log for one low-risk technical problem.
Compare two official help sources before changing a setting or installing software.
Learn one core function in a new tool, produce an output and explain the steps to another learner.
DPS.reflection: Which reversible check will reduce uncertainty without risking data, privacy or device integrity?

AIL.name: AI Literacy
AIL.tagline: Using AI purposefully while preserving verification, privacy, transparency and human judgement
AIL.definition: AI Literacy is confidence in understanding what an AI tool can and cannot do, giving clear instructions, checking outputs, protecting data, recognising bias and keeping humans accountable. It is not permission to use AI in every task or proof of technical AI expertise.
lens: Purpose, context, constraints, evidence, uncertainty, bias, disclosure, privacy and human oversight
Prompt planning, source verification, comparison, error analysis, disclosure and decision review
Automation bias, fabricated sources, privacy leakage, hidden assistance, unfair outcomes or skill atrophy
A lower score may reflect limited safe access or experience; it is not resistance to technology
actions: Give an AI tool a purpose, audience, context and constraints, then identify what remains uncertain.
Verify three factual claims and every cited source using independent evidence.
Create an AI-use note stating the tool, purpose, human changes and verification performed.
AIL.reflection: What evidence, permission and human judgement are still required after the AI output is produced?

bands.label: Emerging
bands.meaning: Create supported exposure and one small practice task

bands.label: Developing
bands.meaning: Build consistency and examine barriers

bands.label: Strong
bands.meaning: Apply in a real task and test balance with other dimensions

bands.label: Highly expressed
bands.meaning: Seek counter-evidence and watch for overuse

OPR.name: Opportunity Recognition
OPR.tagline: Noticing unmet needs and framing possibilities for useful value creation
OPR.definition: Opportunity Recognition is the tendency to notice problems, changes, gaps and underserved needs that may support a useful product, service, process or social solution. It is disciplined attention, not a claim that every idea is commercially viable.
lens: Unmet needs, changing patterns, friction, waste, access gaps and value for others
Problem interviews, observation, trend scanning, need statements and opportunity logs
Falling in love with an idea before checking who has the problem and whether it matters
A lower score may reflect limited exposure, confidence or practice; it does not mean low creativity
actions: Record five repeated problems in one school, household, workplace or community setting.
Interview three people about the problem without pitching a solution.
Write an opportunity statement naming the user, need, present workaround and evidence.
OPR.reflection: What evidence shows that the need is real, repeated and important to someone other than you?

INI.name: Initiative
INI.tagline: Taking an appropriate first step and creating momentum without perfect conditions
INI.definition: Initiative is the tendency to begin useful, proportionate action, seek resources and create a next step when instructions are incomplete. It is not impulsiveness, rule breaking or acting beyond one's competence or authority.
lens: Ownership, first steps, momentum, useful experiments and timely follow-through
Action plans, outreach, small pilots, resource requests and visible commitments
Starting too many activities, bypassing consent or acting before essential safety checks
A lower score may reflect ambiguity, low psychological safety or insufficient support rather than laziness
actions: Define a reversible 30-minute first step for one useful idea.
Ask one specific person for a resource, introduction or piece of feedback.
Set a two-day evidence deadline and record what moved, stalled and why.
INI.reflection: What is the smallest lawful and safe action that will create information or momentum today?

RJK.name: Risk Judgement
RJK.tagline: Distinguishing calculated experiments from careless or irreversible gambles
RJK.definition: Risk Judgement is the tendency to compare potential gains, losses, safeguards and alternatives before acting under uncertainty. A strong score means considered experimentation, not high risk appetite or confidence that losses will not occur.
lens: Downside limits, assumptions, evidence, reversibility, alternatives and stop rules
Pre-mortems, risk registers, small tests, budgets, decision gates and contingency plans
Analysis paralysis at one extreme or overconfidence and avoidable harm at the other
A lower score is a development signal, not proof of irresponsibility or financial incompetence
actions: List the biggest assumption, smallest test, maximum acceptable loss and stop condition.
Separate reversible choices from legal, financial, safety or reputation commitments.
Ask a qualified adult or subject expert to challenge the downside analysis.
RJK.reflection: What could go wrong, how much can be safely lost, and which evidence changes the decision?

RES.name: Resilience
RES.tagline: Learning from setbacks, regulating the response and attempting a thoughtful revision
RES.definition: Resilience is the tendency to maintain perspective, learn from rejection and revise an approach after difficulty. It is not endless persistence, emotional invulnerability or a requirement to tolerate harmful, unsafe or exploitative conditions.
lens: Learning, recovery, perspective, revision, support and evidence-based persistence
After-action reviews, feedback logs, recovery plans, help-seeking and pivot criteria
Treating persistence as a moral test, ignoring wellbeing or continuing an idea after evidence says stop
A lower score may reflect current stress, access barriers or context; it is not a mental-health diagnosis
actions: Separate what happened, what it means and what can be changed next.
Request one behavioural piece of feedback instead of seeking general reassurance.
Choose deliberately among persist, pause, pivot, seek support or stop.
RES.reflection: Which lesson is supported by evidence, and is the responsible next move to persist, pivot or stop?

RSF.name: Resourcefulness
RSF.tagline: Combining available skills, people and materials to progress under constraints
RSF.definition: Resourcefulness is the tendency to find workable alternatives, combine available capabilities and simplify an idea to test its essential value. It does not justify unsafe improvisation, unpaid exploitation, unlicensed content or working beyond competence.
lens: Available means, partners, substitutes, minimum tests, learning and practical trade-offs
Resource maps, prototypes, skill swaps, open resources, constraint redesign and partnerships
Hidden quality or safety compromises, dependency on favours or unauthorised use of others' work
A lower score may reflect limited networks or resources; it is not proof of weak problem-solving ability
actions: Map what you know, whom you can ask and what can be accessed lawfully now.
Remove features until the smallest useful test remains.
Document every borrowed asset, permission, cost, dependency and quality limit.
RSF.reflection: Which existing means can create a responsible test, and where is specialist help non-negotiable?

CUS.name: Customer Orientation
CUS.tagline: Understanding users, testing value and changing direction when evidence requires it
CUS.definition: Customer Orientation is the tendency to understand a user's real problem, define value from the user's perspective and seek feedback before heavy investment. 'Customer' can mean buyer, user, beneficiary or stakeholder, but ethical duties remain distinct.
lens: User context, jobs to be done, evidence, value, accessibility, trust and feedback
Discovery interviews, observation, service journeys, usability tests and feedback loops
Leading interviews, extracting sensitive data, manipulating demand or confusing attention with value
A lower score is a cue to build discovery practice; it does not mean low empathy or social skill
actions: Interview users with neutral questions about current behaviour and workarounds.
Write the strongest evidence against the preferred solution.
Test comprehension, usefulness, accessibility and willingness to act separately.
CUS.reflection: What did users actually do or say, and how did that evidence change the solution?

bands.label: Emerging
bands.meaning: Provide explanation, access and a supported foundation activity

bands.label: Developing
bands.meaning: Practise core behaviours and create one usable artifact

bands.label: Strong
bands.meaning: Test independent application and transfer to a new context

bands.label: Distinctive
bands.meaning: Seek counter-evidence, stretch application and support others carefully

CSA.name: Self-Awareness
CSA.tagline: Understanding strengths, values, skills and development needs through evidence
CSA.definition: Self-Awareness is confidence in describing strengths with examples, recognising skills to develop, explaining important work values and identifying environments in which one performs well. It supports realistic choice without turning a current self-description into a fixed identity.
lens: Strength evidence, transferable skills, values, interests, motivation, preferred conditions and learning needs
Achievement inventories, portfolio review, feedback comparison, skills audits and values reflection
Relying only on praise, confusing aspiration with evidence or treating one assessment label as permanent
A lower score may reflect limited feedback or reflection practice; it is not evidence of low potential
actions: Create an evidence inventory linking five strengths to projects, responsibilities or outcomes.
Compare self-ratings with feedback from two trusted people and note agreements and surprises.
Rank six work values, then explain one realistic trade-off between the top three.
CSA.reflection: Which claim about yourself is supported by evidence, and which still needs testing?

CEX.name: Career Exploration
CEX.tagline: Investigating careers through current information, people, projects and work exposure
CEX.definition: Career Exploration is confidence in researching the daily work behind a title, comparing entry routes and conditions, speaking with informed people and testing possibilities through projects, courses, visits or work exposure. Exploration widens evidence; it does not promise access to every option.
lens: Tasks, work settings, qualifications, skills, demand, progression, conditions, rewards and constraints
Occupational research, informational interviews, career talks, job shadowing, projects and short courses
Choosing by prestige, family pressure, social-media visibility, one success story or outdated information
A lower score may reflect unequal exposure or information access rather than lack of ambition
actions: Compare three pathways using official information on tasks, entry routes, costs, conditions and progression.
Conduct one informational conversation and separate first-hand experience from general advice.
Complete a low-risk project, visit, course or work-exposure activity and record what changed.
CEX.reflection: What new evidence would most reduce uncertainty about this pathway?

CDM.name: Career Decision Making
CDM.tagline: Comparing options with clear criteria and deciding when enough evidence is available
CDM.definition: Career Decision Making is confidence in setting criteria, comparing trade-offs, balancing short-term feasibility with long-term fit, separating useful advice from pressure and making a revisable choice when enough evidence is available. It is structured judgement, not perfect certainty.
lens: Criteria, alternatives, evidence quality, trade-offs, feasibility, reversibility and decision ownership
Decision matrices, scenario testing, advice maps, pre-mortems, checkpoints and contingency routes
Analysis paralysis, premature closure, copying another person's route or treating uncertainty as failure
A lower score may reflect a complex decision or missing information; it is not indecisive character
actions: Build a weighted decision matrix using fit, feasibility, learning, access and future flexibility.
Label each influence as evidence, advice, preference, pressure, constraint or assumption.
Set a decision date, evidence threshold and review point rather than seeking total certainty.
CDM.reflection: Which criterion matters most, and what evidence justifies its weight?

CES.name: Employability Skills
CES.tagline: Using transferable behaviours that support dependable learning and work
CES.definition: Employability Skills is confidence in communicating progress, collaborating across differences, meeting standards, managing deadlines and using feedback to improve. It concerns transferable behaviours across study and work, not technical mastery, job entitlement or employer endorsement.
lens: Communication, teamwork, reliability, self-management, problem solving, feedback use and adaptability
Team projects, role briefs, work simulations, feedback cycles, deadline plans and reflective logs
Making generic skill claims without evidence, overpromising independence or confusing compliance with judgement
A lower score may identify specific habits to practise; it is not a global employability verdict
actions: Complete a team task with a clear role, progress update, deadline and decision record.
Request behavioural feedback, revise the work and show the before-and-after evidence.
Use a weekly plan to meet one agreed quality standard without repeated reminders.
CES.reflection: Which observable behaviour would convince another person that this skill is dependable?

COP.name: Opportunity Preparation
COP.tagline: Preparing truthful, tailored evidence for applications, interviews and opportunities
COP.definition: Opportunity Preparation is confidence in maintaining evidence of projects and achievements, tailoring applications, preparing skill examples and explaining motivation in an interview or professional conversation. It supports opportunity pursuit without guaranteeing selection.
lens: Opportunity fit, eligibility, evidence, truthful claims, tailoring, communication, verification and follow-up
Evidence banks, resumes, applications, portfolios, mock interviews, outreach and opportunity checks
Mass applications, inflated claims, privacy leakage, scam opportunities or hidden AI-generated content
A lower score may reflect limited opportunity access or mentoring; it is not lack of capability
actions: Build six concise situation-action-result examples from genuine projects or responsibilities.
Tailor one resume or application to stated criteria and map every claim to evidence.
Complete a mock interview and verify the organisation, contact, fees, privacy and selection process.
COP.reflection: What evidence shows both that you meet the requirement and that this opportunity is legitimate?

CAP.name: Action Planning
CAP.tagline: Turning goals into dated steps, support routes, evidence and adaptable alternatives
CAP.definition: Action Planning is confidence in translating a career goal into dated next steps, identifying required resources and people, reviewing progress and maintaining an alternative route. It is practical follow-through, not rigid prediction of a changing future.
lens: Goal clarity, milestones, ownership, resources, support, barriers, evidence, review and alternatives
Ninety-day plans, milestone boards, resource maps, implementation intentions and review routines
Vague goals, unrealistic schedules, activity without outcomes, dependency on one route or failure to revise
A lower score is a planning priority; it does not mean the learner lacks motivation or ambition
actions: Create a 90-day plan with weekly actions, owners, evidence, costs and review dates.
Run a pre-mortem to identify likely obstacles, early warning signs and support routes.
Design one alternative education, skill-building or opportunity route that preserves the main goal.
CAP.reflection: What is the next dated action, and what evidence will show that it moved the goal forward?

VER.name: Verbal Reasoning
VER.definition: Understanding relationships, arguments and meaning in written information.
VER.tagline: Understands language, arguments, written evidence and relationships between ideas.
strengths: Reading, explaining, persuading, interpreting and producing clear written or spoken work.
VER.careers: Law; communication; education; policy; consulting; journalism; humanities research.. Example roles: Lawyer; editor; teacher; policy analyst; journalist; communications specialist.
actions: Build domain knowledge and practise concise, audience-specific communication.
VER.watch: Roles dominated by advanced quantitative or mechanical reasoning may require additional preparation.

NUM.name: Numerical Reasoning
NUM.definition: Interpreting quantities, ratios, patterns and numerical evidence.
NUM.tagline: Interprets quantities, ratios, trends and numerical evidence accurately.
strengths: Calculating, modelling, comparing data and making evidence-based financial or operational decisions.
NUM.careers: Finance and accounting; data analysis; economics; engineering; actuarial work; operations.. Example roles: Financial analyst; accountant; data analyst; economist; engineer; operations analyst.
actions: Connect calculations to business meaning and communicate assumptions clearly.
NUM.watch: Language-intensive persuasion or counselling may underuse this strength unless deliberately combined.

LOG.name: Logical and Abstract Reasoning
LOG.definition: Drawing valid conclusions from rules, conditions and sequences.
LOG.tagline: Identifies patterns, rules and valid conclusions in unfamiliar information.
strengths: Complex diagnosis, systems thinking, algorithms and solving novel structured problems.
LOG.careers: Technology and AI; science; engineering; research; strategy; quantitative consulting.. Example roles: Software developer; AI specialist; researcher; systems engineer; strategy analyst.
actions: Test logic against real users, constraints and incomplete evidence.
LOG.watch: Highly repetitive execution may feel under-stimulating when no problem solving is required.

SPA.name: Spatial Reasoning
SPA.definition: Recognising transformations, structures and visual relationships.
SPA.tagline: Mentally visualises shapes, layouts, movement and relationships in space.
strengths: Designing structures, interpreting maps or diagrams and manipulating visual-spatial information.
SPA.careers: Architecture and design; engineering; aviation; geospatial work; animation; surgery and technical imaging.. Example roles: Architect; civil engineer; pilot; GIS analyst; animator; industrial designer.
actions: Develop drawing, CAD, modelling or visualisation tools relevant to the chosen field.
SPA.watch: Work relying mainly on extended verbal interaction may not fully use this ability.

DAT.name: Data Interpretation
DAT.definition: Reading tables, charts and multi-step quantitative information.
DAT.tagline: Combines information from different sources to select practical solutions.
strengths: Diagnosis, trade-off decisions, case analysis and coordinating action under constraints.
DAT.careers: Consulting; medicine; product management; engineering; operations; public policy.. Example roles: Consultant; doctor; product manager; engineer; operations manager; policy analyst.
actions: Make decision criteria explicit and review outcomes to improve judgement.
DAT.watch: Narrow repetitive roles may underuse broad reasoning capacity.

ATT.name: Attention and Accuracy
ATT.definition: Maintaining accuracy, choosing strategies and checking work.
ATT.tagline: Detects errors, maintains concentration and handles detailed information reliably.
strengths: Checking, coding, reviewing records, monitoring quality and following critical procedures.
ATT.careers: Audit and accounting; quality assurance; laboratory work; coding; pharmacy; compliance; operations control.. Example roles: Auditor; QA analyst; laboratory technologist; pharmacist; compliance associate; software tester.
actions: Use risk-based checking so precision is focused where consequences are highest.
ATT.watch: Highly chaotic roles that reward speed over accuracy may create conflict or fatigue.
